column3: It immediately completes the same prophet list by calling all of them excellent, directly repeating the focus's final quality.
The incomplete report that they used to speak supplies no content about divine choosing or excellence.
Its false claim that God chose daughters over sons contrasts with the genuine divine choosing affirmed in the focus.
David's honored standing with God parallels the focus's "with Us" evaluation, though it emphasizes return rather than election.
It introduces Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God's servants immediately before the focus's judgment on them.
God's choosing of Adam, Noah, and Abraham's and Imran's families directly establishes divine election.
The wish for an earlier reminder uses "with us" in an unrelated human sense.
The lasting home of the hereafter supplies the ultimate horizon for divine judgments of worth.
What is better with the Lord reorients value toward divine reward, without directly describing chosen servants.
David's forgiveness and nearness with God echo the focus's divine evaluation but do not name election or excellence.
It immediately gives the divine act that set these servants apart for remembrance of the final abode.

The shared mortality of the Prophet and his opponents does not clarify the focus's praise.

Seeking refuge from satanic prompting does not address divine choosing or excellence.
God's intended replacement with one better, purer, and more merciful supplies a related measure of betterment.

God as the best of the merciful establishes divine perfection behind the focus's favorable judgment.
God alone knows inner selves and may give good, only loosely relating divine judgment to worth.
The abode of peace with their Lord presents a settled blessed outcome for those rightly guided.

God's chosen servants are explicitly named in praise, directly echoing the focus's chosen excellence.
Sincere devotion to God supplies the servant orientation associated with authentic divine favor.
God's reward is better for believers who do good, relating excellence to faith, action, and patience.
Good known in hearts brings a better return and forgiveness, but the verse does not speak of election.

God as the best provider locates all true provision in the divine source of goodness.
The possibility of receiving a better garden concerns divine replacement, not chosen servants.
Victory for God's forces does not clarify the personal divine election in the focus.
The mistaken assumption that worldly goods mean accelerated good warns against equating prosperity with favor.
The Prophet's designation as a messenger provides a related instance of divine commissioning.
Preventing good supplies the negative moral opposite of the excellence attributed in the focus.
Nearness granted by Pharaoh gives a limited contrast to the focus's true honored standing with God.

The remaining sign for those who fear punishment does not address choosing or excellence.
Those who bring good receive something better, showing divine recompense that exceeds good action.
Elijah is identified as one of God's believing servants, a related prophetic commendation.
Patience being better offers a narrow ethical comparison without an election theme.
Noah is identified as one of God's believing servants, a related prophetic commendation.
Believing servants seek the mercy of the best merciful, joining servant identity to divine grace.
Divine power to show a promised punishment does not explain chosen excellence.
Hoarding good when it arrives describes possessiveness, only a loose negative contrast to excellence.
Noah's status among God's believing servants parallels the focus's praise of prophetic servants.
God as the best protector and most merciful is a broad divine-perfection parallel.
The anguish of the affluent under punishment does not address divine election.
Solomon's love of prized goods displacing remembrance warns that valued things must not displace devotion to God.
The explanation of signs so people may return gives no distinct account of election.

The isolated opening letters provide no interpretable link to the focus's theme.
God as the best giver of lodging frames divine favor as secure, beneficent placement.
All treasuries being with God establishes divine custody and measured bestowal, not servant election itself.
Those who hasten in good works offer an active model of the excellence praised in the focus.
A servant given mercy and knowledge from God illustrates distinctive divine favor toward a servant.
The hereafter being better and more enduring gives a lasting criterion for true excellence.
God's knowledgeable choosing of Israel is an explicit parallel to the focus's divine election.

The later state being better than the first presents a divine pattern of enduring betterment.
Job's restoration through mercy from God shows distinguished divine care for an exemplary servant.
God's recompense being better and His provision unsurpassed establishes divine superiority as the measure of good.
The violent response to truth from God does not illuminate divine choosing or excellence.
Open or hidden good and forgiveness offer a general ethical parallel without election.

Expecting to meet and return to the Lord supplies a broad final-accountability context.

The claim that people may choose whatever they wish from a book does not address divine election.
The Night of Decree being better than a thousand months shows divinely assigned superiority, though not chosen servants.
The correction of regretful claims about death has no useful relation to election or excellence.
Intercession only by God's permission gives a limited picture of access to God, not chosen excellence.
The legal procedure for spousal accusation does not clarify the focus's themes.
Settlement in the land for those who fear God offers a broad moral outcome, not election.
The warning that defrauders will be resurrected does not concern chosen servants.
The final division into wretched and happy gives a broad contrast to divine favorable judgment.

Communal unity as divine favor provides a broad positive outcome but no direct election theme.
The signs in natural cycles do not identify chosen or excellent servants.
The household eating permissions and greeting do not bear on the focus's divine evaluation.
Its challenge to claims of being better shows that superiority is judged by God and historical accountability.
God's favoring of Israel above the peoples gives a communal precedent for divinely conferred distinction.

God's choice of Talut, confirmed by knowledge and stature, directly presents election as a divine judgment rather than popular preference.
Jesus is announced as honored in this world and the next and among those brought near, a related pattern of divine honor.
God singles out whom He wills for mercy, directly grounding distinction in divine choice.
The community is called the best raised for humanity, a broader communal form of excellence without the focus's election language.
God chooses whom He wills from among His messengers, directly linking election to prophetic mission.
The people God loves and who love Him provide a related portrait of divinely favored, morally excellent servants.
A group of prophets, including Ishmael, Elisha, and Lot, is explicitly preferred above the worlds.
God's choosing and guiding of the prophets directly parallels the focus's description of selected servants.
Moses is chosen above people for God's messages and speech, an explicit instance of prophetic election.

Joseph is identified as one of God's devoted servants, a related description of exceptional servant status.
Abraham is explicitly chosen and guided to a straight path, closely paralleling the focus's praise of him.
God's preference of some prophets over others supplies a direct prophetic hierarchy of divine favor.
Mercy and a lofty truthful renown are granted to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, extending their divine commendation.
The prophets are explicitly described as those upon whom God bestowed favor.
God tells Moses that He has chosen him, an unambiguous parallel to the focus's election language.
Adam's Lord chose him, turned toward him, and guided him, directly joining election with restored favor.
The angels are called honored servants, offering a close parallel to the focus's excellent servant status.
God chooses messengers from angels and humanity, directly defining election as divine appointment.
God creates what He wills and chooses, stating the divine prerogative underlying the focus's selected servants.
God appoints guiding leaders from among a people in response to patience and certainty, linking distinction with faithful endurance.
The household's purification presents a related form of divine setting apart and moral refinement.
Moses is described as honored in God's sight, closely paralleling the focus's "with Us" divine evaluation.

The repeated exception for God's chosen servants reinforces their protected, distinguished status.
Elijah's story again identifies God's chosen servants, directly linking prophetic fidelity with election.
The final repetition of God's chosen servants confirms the category applied to the focus's prophets.
Iblis excepts God's chosen servants from his power, directly naming their protected, selected status in the same surah.
God chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides them to Himself, directly connecting election and divine orientation.
God gives His bounty to whom He wills, a broad divine-favor parallel without explicit selection of servants.
Jonah's Lord chose him and made him righteous, directly combining election with restored moral excellence.
